market_context: United States/general English; handling raw chicken and preventing kitchen cross-contamination
title: Should you wash chicken before cooking?

seo.title: Should you wash raw chicken before cooking?
seo.meta_description: No. Washing raw chicken does not make it safer and can spread bacteria around the sink and kitchen. Cook poultry to 165 °F instead.
seo.search_intent: Learn why USDA advises against washing raw chicken and what to do instead for safe handling.

excerpt: USDA advises against washing raw poultry. Running water can splash bacteria from chicken onto the sink, faucet, counters, utensils or ready-to-eat food. Safe handling and cooking to at least 165 °F in the thickest part are more effective than rinsing.
content_html:
Running water over raw chicken does not sterilize it. USDA advises against washing poultry because splashes can spread bacteria around the kitchen.

Why washing can increase risk

Water hitting raw poultry can carry microorganisms to the sink, faucet, counters, utensils and nearby foods. The chicken may look cleaner while the kitchen becomes harder to keep clean.

Vinegar, lemon and salt water are not safety substitutes

Soaking or rinsing may be part of a recipe or family tradition, but it is not a reliable pathogen-control step. USDA states that rinsing, washing or soaking is unnecessary for safety.

Heat is the reliable control

Chicken should reach at least 165 °F (73.9 °C) in the thickest appropriate area, measured with a food thermometer.

What to do instead

  • Open the package without splashing raw juices.
  • If browning matters, pat the surface dry with disposable paper towels.
  • Wash hands with soap after handling raw chicken.
  • Clean and sanitize utensils and surfaces that contacted raw poultry.
  • Keep chicken and its juices away from ready-to-eat foods.

If you already washed it

You do not need to throw the chicken away. Clean and sanitize the sink, faucet, counters and anything reached by splashes, wash your hands and cook the chicken properly.

Washing raw chicken feels intuitive because rinsing is associated with cleaning, but poultry is one of the clearest cases where that instinct works against food safety. Water does not reliably remove pathogens from the meat, and splashes can carry contaminated droplets to the sink, faucet, nearby utensils, dish towels and ready-to-eat foods. USDA research and guidance therefore recommend not washing raw poultry. The safety step that actually kills harmful bacteria is thorough cooking to a safe internal temperature, combined with careful hand washing and separation of raw poultry from foods that will not be cooked.

The splash zone is larger than it looks. A gentle stream of water can send tiny droplets beyond the sink basin, and those droplets are easy to miss during routine cleanup. Adding vinegar, lemon juice or salt water does not make rinsing a dependable decontamination method. Marinades can change flavor or texture, but they should not be treated as sanitizers. If raw chicken has visible bone fragments or packaging liquid, use clean paper towel only when truly necessary, discard it immediately and then clean and sanitize the contacted surfaces rather than putting the bird under running water.

A better workflow starts before the package is opened. Keep raw chicken on the lowest refrigerator shelf in a leak-proof container, prepare salad or other ready-to-eat ingredients first, and use a separate cutting board if possible. After handling the poultry, wash hands with soap and water and clean knives, boards, counters and sink areas that may have been touched. Avoid touching spice jars or refrigerator handles with contaminated hands. These small habits interrupt cross-contamination much more effectively than trying to 'wash away' bacteria from the chicken itself.

Cooking completes the safety chain. Use a food thermometer in the thickest part and follow the appropriate safe minimum internal temperature rather than judging doneness only by color or clear juices. Once cooked, place the chicken on a clean plate, not the one that held it raw. The practical message is simple: raw chicken does not need a bath. Keep its juices contained, keep your hands and work surfaces clean, and let heat—not the kitchen tap—do the job of destroying pathogens.

Water does not remove the risk; it can move it

The problem with washing raw chicken is not that water makes the meat more dangerous. Splashes can move microorganisms from the surface to the sink, counter, utensils or ready-to-eat foods. Thorough cooking is the step designed to control that hazard. If there is visible package liquid, handle it carefully rather than turning the sink into a raw-meat washing station.

Do not wash chicken to make it safe. Prevent cross-contamination and use a thermometer during cooking.

faq.question: Does vinegar kill bacteria on raw chicken?
faq.answer: Not reliably enough to replace safe cooking. USDA does not recommend washing or soaking poultry for safety.

faq.question: Can I pat chicken dry?
faq.answer: Yes. Use disposable paper towel, discard it immediately and wash your hands afterward.

faq.question: What temperature should chicken reach?
faq.answer: At least 165 °F in the thickest part, measured with a food thermometer.
